Monthly Sales Forecasting: Classical Statistics + Time-Aware Validation¶

Goal: Forecast the next 12 months of sales, and be honest about how much to trust that forecast.

Dataset: Monthly car sales in Quebec, Jan 1960 - Dec 1968 (108 observations). A real, public series with trend and strong seasonality.

What this notebook demonstrates

  1. Data quality checks and exploratory analysis
  2. Statistical tests (stationarity, autocorrelation, residual normality)
  3. Proper time-series validation (no shuffling, no leakage; rolling-origin CV)
  4. Baselines vs. classical models vs. a feature-based ML model
  5. Residual diagnostics and prediction intervals
  6. Applicability and limitations of the data and the conclusions

Outline: 1 Load & quality checks, 2 EDA, 3 Statistical tests, 4 Validation design, 5 Models, 6 Results, 7 Diagnostics, 8 Final forecast, 9 Applicability & limitations

In [1]:
import warnings
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
import itertools

warnings.simplefilter("ignore")   # statsmodels emits many convergence notices during the AIC grid search
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid"); plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (11, 4)
SEED = 42; np.random.seed(SEED)

What the EDA shows

  • Trend: sales rise strongly through 1965, dip slightly in 1966-67 (annual totals -2.2% and -0.9%), then recover in 1968 (+9.9%). Growth is not steady, which matters for extrapolation.
  • Seasonality: a repeating annual pattern (strongest months and weakest months are consistent year to year).
  • Changing amplitude: seasonal swings grow as the level grows, a multiplicative pattern. This is why we will test a log transform below.
In [5]:
# Decompose with STL (robust, handles evolving seasonality). Use log so effects are additive.
stl = STL(np.log(s), period=12, robust=True).fit()
fig = stl.plot(); fig.set_size_inches(11, 7); plt.show()

strength_trend = max(0, 1 - stl.resid.var()/(stl.trend+stl.resid).var())
strength_seas  = max(0, 1 - stl.resid.var()/(stl.seasonal+stl.resid).var())
print(f"Strength of trend: {strength_trend:.2f} | Strength of seasonality: {strength_seas:.2f}  (0 = none, 1 = dominant)")

Strength of trend: 0.87 | Strength of seasonality: 0.91  (0 = none, 1 = dominant)

3. Statistical tests¶

3.1 Stationarity¶

Most classical models assume the statistical properties of the series don't drift over time. We use two tests with opposite null hypotheses, so agreement between them is more convincing:

  • ADF: H0 = series has a unit root (non-stationary). Small p-value -> stationary.
  • KPSS: H0 = series is stationary. Small p-value -> non-stationary.
In [6]:
def stationarity(x, name):
    adf_p = adfuller(x.dropna(), autolag="AIC")[1]
    kpss_p = kpss(x.dropna(), regression="c", nlags="auto")[1]
    return {"series": name, "ADF p (want <0.05)": round(adf_p,4), "KPSS p (want >0.05)": round(kpss_p,4),
            "verdict": "stationary" if (adf_p<0.05 and kpss_p>0.05) else "NOT stationary"}

ls = np.log(s)
rows = [stationarity(s, "raw"),
        stationarity(ls, "log"),
        stationarity(ls.diff(12), "log, seasonal diff (12)"),
        stationarity(ls.diff(12).diff(1), "log, seasonal + regular diff")]
pd.DataFrame(rows)
Out[6]:
series ADF p (want <0.05) KPSS p (want >0.05) verdict
0 raw 0.6633 0.01 NOT stationary
1 log 0.5569 0.01 NOT stationary
2 log, seasonal diff (12) 0.0002 0.10 stationary
3 log, seasonal + regular diff 0.0076 0.10 stationary

Interpretation: The raw series is not stationary (trend + seasonality). Differencing removes this. That tells us SARIMA needs differencing (d and/or D > 0), which guides the model search below. We don't just trust a tool to figure this out; the tests tell us why.

3.2 Variance stabilisation (is the log transform justified?)¶

In [7]:
# If seasonal swings scale with the level, std-dev across years should grow with the mean (multiplicative).
yr = s.groupby(s.index.year).agg(["mean","std"])
yr["cv"] = yr["std"]/yr["mean"]
r = stats.pearsonr(yr["mean"], yr["std"])
print(yr.round(1).to_string()); print(f"\nCorrelation between yearly mean and yearly std: r = {r[0]:.2f} (p={r[1]:.4f})")
print(f"Mean yearly coefficient of variation: {yr['cv'].mean():.2f}")
print("Evidence is moderate (r=0.64, p~0.06, n=9 years), not conclusive. The log transform is still a reasonable, low-risk choice: it also keeps forecasts positive.")

3.3 Autocorrelation structure (ACF / PACF)¶

In [8]:
w = ls.diff(12).diff(1).dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
plot_acf(w, lags=36, ax=ax[0]); plot_pacf(w, lags=36, ax=ax[1], method="ywm")
ax[0].set_title("ACF (log, seasonally+regularly differenced)"); ax[1].set_title("PACF")
plt.show()

Reading the plots: spikes at lag 1 and at lag 12 (seasonal lag) suggest small non-seasonal and seasonal MA/AR terms, i.e. a SARIMA of the form (p,1,q)(P,1,Q)[12] is a sensible candidate family. We'll search a small grid around that using AIC on training data only.

4. Validation design (the part many projects get wrong)¶

Random train/test splits leak the future into training for time-series data. Instead:

  1. Hold-out test set: the final 12 months. Touched once, at the end.
  2. Rolling-origin cross-validation on the earlier data: train on everything up to a cutoff, forecast the next 12 months, then move the cutoff forward 12 months. This gives several honest error estimates rather than one lucky/unlucky number.
  3. Metrics: MAE and RMSE (units), MAPE (interpretable %), and MASE (error scaled against a seasonal-naive forecast; <1 means we beat the naive baseline).
In [9]:
H = 12
train, test = s.iloc[:-H], s.iloc[-H:]
print(f"Train: {train.index.min().date()} -> {train.index.max().date()} ({len(train)} months)")
print(f"Test : {test.index.min().date()} -> {test.index.max().date()} ({len(test)} months)")

def mase(y, yhat, y_train, m=12):
    scale = np.mean(np.abs(y_train.values[m:] - y_train.values[:-m]))
    return np.mean(np.abs(y.values - yhat))/scale

def metrics(y, yhat, y_train):
    y, yhat = np.asarray(y), np.asarray(yhat)
    return {"MAE": np.mean(np.abs(y-yhat)), "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((y-yhat)**2)),
            "MAPE%": np.mean(np.abs((y-yhat)/y))*100, "MASE": mase(pd.Series(y), yhat, y_train)}

Train: 1960-01-01 -> 1967-12-01 (96 months)
Test : 1968-01-01 -> 1968-12-01 (12 months)

5. Models¶

Ordered from simplest to most complex. A fancy model must beat the simple ones to justify itself.

Model Idea
Naive tomorrow = today. Floor for any forecast
Seasonal naive this month = same month last year. Strong baseline for seasonal data
Holt-Winters (ETS) smooth level + trend + seasonality, fitted on log scale
SARIMA autoregressive/moving-average model with differencing, orders chosen by AIC on training data
Gradient boosting ML model on engineered features (lags, month, trend); tests whether ML adds value
In [10]:
# ---- forecasting functions: each takes a training series and horizon, returns point forecasts (original scale)
def f_naive(tr, h):          return np.repeat(tr.iloc[-1], h)
def f_snaive(tr, h):         return tr.iloc[-12:].values[np.arange(h) % 12]

def f_hw(tr, h):
    m = ExponentialSmoothing(np.log(tr), trend="add", damped_trend=True, seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=12).fit()
    return np.exp(m.forecast(h)).values

def pick_sarima(tr, grid_p=(0,1,2), grid_q=(0,1,2), grid_P=(0,1), grid_Q=(0,1)):
    best = (np.inf, None)
    for p,q,P,Q in itertools.product(grid_p, grid_q, grid_P, grid_Q):
        try:
            r = SARIMAX(np.log(tr), order=(p,1,q), seasonal_order=(P,1,Q,12)).fit(disp=False)
            if r.aic < best[0]: best = (r.aic, (p,1,q,P,1,Q))
        except Exception: pass
    return best

SARIMA_ORDER = None   # chosen once on training data only, to avoid leaking test info
def f_sarima(tr, h):
    p,d,q,P,D,Q = SARIMA_ORDER
    r = SARIMAX(np.log(tr), order=(p,d,q), seasonal_order=(P,D,Q,12)).fit(disp=False)
    return np.exp(r.forecast(h)).values

# ---- ML model: recursive forecasting with lag features
def make_features(series):
    X = pd.DataFrame({"lag1": series.shift(1), "lag2": series.shift(2), "lag3": series.shift(3),
                      "lag12": series.shift(12), "roll3": series.shift(1).rolling(3).mean(),
                      "roll12": series.shift(1).rolling(12).mean(), "month": series.index.month})
    return X

def f_gbm(tr, h):
    ly = np.log(tr)
    X = make_features(ly); y = ly
    mask = X.notna().all(axis=1)
    model = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8, random_state=SEED)
    model.fit(X[mask], y[mask])
    hist = ly.copy(); preds = []
    for i in range(h):
        nxt = hist.index[-1] + pd.offsets.MonthBegin(1)
        tmp = pd.concat([hist, pd.Series([np.nan], index=[nxt])])
        xrow = make_features(tmp).iloc[[-1]]
        yhat = model.predict(xrow)[0]
        hist = pd.concat([hist, pd.Series([yhat], index=[nxt])]); preds.append(yhat)
    return np.exp(preds)

# choose SARIMA order using the training portion only
aic, SARIMA_ORDER = pick_sarima(train)
print("Selected SARIMA (p,d,q)(P,D,Q)[12] on log scale:", SARIMA_ORDER[:3], SARIMA_ORDER[3:], "| AIC =", round(aic,1))

MODELS = {"Naive": f_naive, "Seasonal naive": f_snaive, "Holt-Winters (damped)": f_hw,
          "SARIMA": f_sarima, "Gradient boosting": f_gbm}

Selected SARIMA (p,d,q)(P,D,Q)[12] on log scale: (2, 1, 1) (1, 1, 1) | AIC = -108.9

5.1 Rolling-origin cross-validation (on training data only)¶

In [11]:
origins = [48, 60, 72, 84]   # months of history available at each fold; each fold forecasts the next 12 months
cv_rows = []
for name, fn in MODELS.items():
    for o in origins:
        tr, va = train.iloc[:o], train.iloc[o:o+H]
        if len(va) < H: continue
        yhat = fn(tr, H)
        cv_rows.append({"model": name, "origin": o, **metrics(va, yhat, tr)})
cv = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows)
cv_summary = cv.groupby("model")[["MAE","RMSE","MAPE%","MASE"]].agg(["mean","std"]).round(2)
cv_mean = cv.groupby("model")[["MAE","RMSE","MAPE%","MASE"]].mean().round(2).sort_values("MAPE%")
print("Mean CV performance across", len(origins), "rolling folds (lower is better):"); cv_mean

Mean CV performance across 4 rolling folds (lower is better):

In [12]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9,4))
sns.barplot(data=cv, x="model", y="MAPE%", errorbar="sd", color="steelblue", ax=ax, order=cv_mean.index)
ax.set_title("Cross-validated MAPE by model (bars = mean, whiskers = std across folds)"); plt.xticks(rotation=15); plt.show()

Key finding: in cross-validation the seasonal-naive baseline is the best model (MASE ~ 0.99), ahead of Holt-Winters, SARIMA and gradient boosting. The more complex models do not clearly earn their complexity on the training-period folds. Naive (no seasonality) is far worse, so seasonality is where nearly all the forecastable signal lives.

Note on variance: with only 4 folds, differences between close models are within noise. We report the std across folds for that reason. Ranking models on one test window alone would overstate our confidence.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,5))
tr36 = train.iloc[-36:]
ax.plot(tr36.index, tr36.values, color="gray", label="Train (last 3 yrs)")
ax.plot(test.index, test.values, color="black", lw=2.5, label="Actual (test)")
for n, p in preds.items(): ax.plot(test.index, p, marker="o", ms=3, label=n, alpha=.85)
ax.set_title("Hold-out forecasts vs actual"); ax.set_ylabel("Units")
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 0.5)); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Honest reading of the two evaluations: on the final hold-out, SARIMA is best (MAPE ~ 7.8%, MASE 0.91), while in rolling CV it ranked behind seasonal naive. Two different evaluation windows disagree about the winner. That is expected with ~100 points: model rankings here are unstable, and the hold-out is a single 12-month window, so it should not be over-interpreted. A defensible conclusion is: seasonality-aware models forecast far better than a naive one; SARIMA is competitive and offers prediction intervals; but its edge over seasonal naive is not proven.

How to read this: MASE < 1 means the model beats a seasonal-naive forecast on the training scale. If a complex model does not beat seasonal naive meaningfully, the simpler model is the better engineering choice, since it is easier to explain, cheaper, and less likely to break.

7. Residual diagnostics of the best statistical model¶

In [15]:
best_name = results.drop(index=["Naive","Gradient boosting"], errors="ignore").index[0]
print("Diagnosing:", best_name)
if best_name == "SARIMA":
    p,d,q,P,D,Q = SARIMA_ORDER
    fit = SARIMAX(np.log(train), order=(p,d,q), seasonal_order=(P,D,Q,12)).fit(disp=False)
    resid = fit.resid.iloc[13:]
else:
    fit = ExponentialSmoothing(np.log(train), trend="add", damped_trend=True, seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=12).fit()
    resid = fit.resid.iloc[13:]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16,4))
resid.plot(ax=ax[0], title="Residuals over time"); ax[0].axhline(0, color="k", lw=.8)
plot_acf(resid, lags=24, ax=ax[1], title="Residual ACF")
sm.qqplot(resid, line="s", ax=ax[2]); ax[2].set_title("Q-Q plot (normality)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

lb = acorr_ljungbox(resid, lags=[12, 24], return_df=True)
sw = stats.shapiro(resid)
print("Ljung-Box (H0: residuals are uncorrelated; want p>0.05):"); print(lb.round(3))
print(f"\nShapiro-Wilk normality: W={sw.statistic:.3f}, p={sw.pvalue:.3f}  (want p>0.05)")
print(f"Residual mean: {resid.mean():.4f} (want ~0)")

Diagnosing: SARIMA

Ljung-Box (H0: residuals are uncorrelated; want p>0.05):
    lb_stat  lb_pvalue
12   10.610      0.563
24   26.396      0.333

Shapiro-Wilk normality: W=0.974, p=0.093  (want p>0.05)
Residual mean: -0.0103 (want ~0)

Results: Ljung-Box p-values (0.56 at lag 12, 0.33 at lag 24) show no remaining autocorrelation, residual mean is near zero, and Shapiro-Wilk (p ~ 0.09) does not reject normality, though only marginally. The model passes its checks, which supports using its intervals, with the caveat that these tests have low power on ~100 points.

Why this matters: If residuals still contain autocorrelation, the model has missed structure and its prediction intervals will be too narrow. If residuals are non-normal, interval coverage claims are weaker. Passing these checks is what justifies reporting intervals; failing them should be disclosed (see limitations).

8. Final forecast: next 12 months (Jan - Dec 1969) with prediction intervals¶

In [16]:
# Refit on ALL data, then forecast beyond the observed range
aic_full, order_full = pick_sarima(s)
p,d,q,P,D,Q = order_full
final = SARIMAX(np.log(s), order=(p,d,q), seasonal_order=(P,D,Q,12)).fit(disp=False)
fc = final.get_forecast(H); ci = fc.conf_int(alpha=0.20)   # 80% interval
idx = pd.date_range(s.index[-1] + pd.offsets.MonthBegin(1), periods=H, freq="MS")
fdf = pd.DataFrame({"forecast": np.exp(fc.predicted_mean.values),
                    "lower_80": np.exp(ci.iloc[:,0].values), "upper_80": np.exp(ci.iloc[:,1].values)}, index=idx).round(0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,5))
s.iloc[-48:].plot(ax=ax, color="black", label="History")
fdf["forecast"].plot(ax=ax, color="crimson", marker="o", label="Forecast")
ax.fill_between(fdf.index, fdf["lower_80"], fdf["upper_80"], color="crimson", alpha=.2, label="80% prediction interval")
ax.set_title(f"12-month forecast, SARIMA{order_full[:3]}x{order_full[3:]}[12] on log scale"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
print("Selected order on full data:", order_full); fdf

# Does the 80% interval actually cover ~80% of the time? Check on the hold-out using the train-only model.
p,d,q,P,D,Q = SARIMA_ORDER
m = SARIMAX(np.log(train), order=(p,d,q), seasonal_order=(P,D,Q,12)).fit(disp=False)
c = m.get_forecast(H).conf_int(alpha=0.20)
inside = ((np.log(test.values) >= c.iloc[:,0].values) & (np.log(test.values) <= c.iloc[:,1].values)).mean()
print(f"Empirical coverage of the nominal 80% interval on hold-out: {inside*100:.0f}%  (12 points only, so very noisy)")

Empirical coverage of the nominal 80% interval on hold-out: 83%  (12 points only, so very noisy)

Reading the forecast: the model projects a seasonal peak in spring (about 28k units in May 1969) and a trough in winter/early autumn. The 80% interval is roughly +/-15-17% around each point forecast, so planning should use the range, not just the line. The hold-out coverage check (83% vs 80% nominal) looks fine but rests on 12 points, so it is weak evidence.

9. Applicability and limitations¶

Where this analysis is applicable¶

  • Short-horizon planning (up to ~12 months) of aggregate monthly demand for a product line with stable seasonal behaviour: inventory, staffing, and budget baselines.
  • Benchmarking: the methodology (leak-free validation, baselines first, diagnostics, intervals) transfers directly to other sales series. The specific model orders do not.
  • Explaining drivers: the decomposition and seasonal indices give business-readable insight (which months peak, how fast the trend is growing).

Limitations of the data¶

  1. Small sample. 108 monthly points with only 9 complete seasonal cycles. Seasonal parameters are estimated from very few repetitions, and CV folds are few, so model rankings are noisy.
  2. Old and single-market. 1960s Quebec; consumer behaviour, pricing, financing and competition differ greatly today. Nothing here should be read as a modern forecast.
  3. Univariate. No price, promotion, macroeconomic, weather, or competitor variables, so the model cannot explain why sales move or react to planned interventions (e.g., a discount).
  4. Aggregated. Total monthly sales hide differences across products, regions and customer segments; forecasts do not apply to a single SKU or store.
  5. No documentation of data collection. We cannot verify definitions (units vs. revenue, returns, reporting changes).

Limitations of the modelling¶

  1. Assumes the future resembles the past (stable seasonality and smooth trend). Structural breaks (recession, new competitor, product launch, pandemic) would invalidate the forecast, and prediction intervals do not account for them.
  2. Prediction intervals assume well-behaved residuals (roughly normal, uncorrelated, constant variance on log scale). Diagnostics in Section 7 check this, but with ~100 points the tests have limited power.
  3. Order selection by AIC on a small grid adds model-selection uncertainty that the reported intervals ignore.
  4. Hold-out of 12 points gives a high-variance estimate of true error; the interval coverage check is based on only 12 observations.
  5. Gradient boosting struggles with short series and trend extrapolation: tree models cannot predict values outside the range seen in training, which is a structural weakness for trending data.
  6. Recursive multi-step forecasting (used for the ML model) compounds errors with horizon.
  7. Model ranking is unstable. CV and hold-out disagree on whether SARIMA beats seasonal naive (see Section 6). A production system would keep seasonal naive as a permanent benchmark and only adopt a complex model if it wins consistently.
  8. Optimizer convergence. Some SARIMA fits in the AIC grid search raised convergence warnings (suppressed above for readability). A more careful workflow would exclude or re-fit non-converged candidates.
  9. Level/log transform trade-off: forecasting on the log scale and exponentiating gives the median, not the mean; for planning in units this introduces a small downward bias.

What I would do next with more time/data¶

  • Add external regressors (price, promotions, economic indicators) via SARIMAX or gradient boosting with proper lagged features.
  • Hierarchical forecasting (by product/region) and reconciliation.
  • Use more folds on a longer history; try conformal prediction for distribution-free intervals.
  • Monitor forecast error in production and retrain when bias appears.

Conclusion¶

Seasonality explains most of the forecastable variation: every seasonal method beats the non-seasonal naive baseline by a wide margin (MAPE ~8-12% vs ~21-22%). SARIMA was best on the hold-out and has well-behaved residuals, but it did not beat seasonal naive in cross-validation, so the honest takeaway is that a simple seasonal baseline is hard to beat on a series this short. Modelling choices (log transform, differencing, seasonal period) were justified by tests, models were compared on leak-free rolling validation, and the forecast ships with uncertainty and stated limits.
